newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African cabinet report on oil pricing due soon.
newsitem.headline: S.African cabinet report on oil pricing due soon.

text.p: An inter-ministerial study into the future of domestic oil prices could be completed by the end of November, South African Minerals and Energy Affairs Minister Penuell Maduna said on Wednesday.
"All things being equal this should be over by the end of this month," Maduna told a media briefing.
"But then, again, we have all sorts of commitments including trips abroad, which are also very critical, and that may impact on time frames."

The Cabinet last month appointed a special committee to review the government's position on the marketing of petroleum activities return mechanisms (MPAR), as well as possible amendments to the oil price formula.
This follows a plea from the oil industry for a three cents a litre wholesale margin increase, the first since September 1993.
The committee consists Maduna, Transport Minister Mac Maharaj, Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Trade and Industry Minister Alec Erwin.

In terms of the MPAR, the oil industry has been due for a wholesale margin increase since January this year and it had hoped that it would be granted an increase in the gasoline price adjustment on November 6.
"We have teams that are actually working and they are reporting to us on all sorts of problems," Maduna said.
These included the MPAR and the In Bond Landed Cost (IBLC) formula on which petrol prices were calculated.
"When we think we are ready, we will make an announcement but we want to be fair to the industry and we will go to them and have discussions with them," Maduna said.
"We are not going to seek to impose our own ideas on them. They have invested in the industry and we would want to ensure that they are not treated shabbily."

Maduna said that the report on the oil industry by University of Stellenbosch academic Izak Lamprechts had been submitted to tripartite Nedlac body -- grouping busijness, government and labour -- for discussion and he did not want to pre-empt anything it might come up with.

The oil industry has warned that important investment decisions, including refinery expansions to meet growing demand, hang in the balance and that greater certainty about government's attitude to the oil industry, including pricing, is needed urgenty.
